speaker: Doctor
text: Can you tell me if you have any history of trauma, infection, or similar joint issues in this knee before? Also, does the pain wake you up at night or improve with rest?

speaker: Patient
text: 24-year-old male. The patient reports increasing pain and swelling of the left knee over 2 months. Describes the pain as severe enough to awaken him from sleep on several occasions. States he tried taking ibuprofen with no relief. No family or personal history of significant illnesses.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has the swelling been present since the very beginning, or did it appear gradually after a specific event? Additionally, is there any redness or warmth you can feel when you touch the knee?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Severe pain and swelling in the left knee. I also have Pain intensifying over 2 months, Painful awakenings during night, No relief with ibuprofen. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Urinary tract infection and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is highly unusual; a Urinary Tract Infection would not present with isolated knee pain and swelling. Given your age and the severe night pain, have you noticed any recent trauma, or is the knee stiff in the morning? Also, has anyone examined the joint or ordered X-rays to rule out structural causes?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: Non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially. Engineer by profession.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Left Knee X-Ray (AP, Lateral, and Sunrise views). REQUEST IMAGES: None yet needed, please await X-ray results. Can you describe what you do for work as an engineer and if your job involves heavy lifting or repetitive kneeling?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: X-Ray Left Knee: A lytic lesion in the distal femur near the knee joint with a thin rim of bone on the external surface and a 'soap bubble' appearance.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Giant Cell Tumor of the Distal Femur.

This lytic lesion with a "soap bubble" appearance is characteristic of this benign but locally aggressive bone tumor, often affecting young adults near the knee joint. Given the night pain and swelling, we need to rule out malignant transformation or fracture risk. I recommend an MRI of the left knee to assess the soft tissue extent and a CT scan if surgical planning is required.
